name: Gene doping

lead: Gene doping is the non-therapeutic use of gene therapy to improve athletic performance, for example by adding genes that raise muscle growth or red-cell production. Wikipedia reports that as of 2024 there is no evidence it has been used in any sporting event.

It appears in physique discussion because animal research on genes such as myostatin, follistatin and IGF-1 produced very muscular animals, suggesting a way past natural muscle limits. Human use for appearance has not been documented, and the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) has banned the practice.

paras: It is not a practice available to the public; it exists as animal and early clinical research on gene therapy. WADA funds detection research, including PCR and sequencing methods that look for added genetic material.

Gene-therapy trials have shown risks including immune reactions, insertional mutagenesis that can lead to cancer, and death, as in the 1999 Jesse Gelsinger case. Animal work on EPO overexpression produced organ damage and anemia in some animals.

angle.text: The appeal is muscle growth beyond natural limits via genes such as myostatin inhibitors. It remains animal and early clinical research and is banned in sport.

lead: Gene doping refers to the non-therapeutic use of gene therapy or gene-editing to enhance athletic performance. WADA added gene doping to its banned list in the early 2000s, and funded detection research from 2004.[1]

The idea draws on animal research: mice overexpressing IGF-1 (published 1998) became more muscular, removing or limiting myostatin increases muscle size, and follistatin gene therapy produced muscle growth in primates in 2009.[1] EPO gene insertion raised hematocrit sharply in mice and monkeys but caused autoimmune anemia in some animals.[1]
For people interested in physique, it represents a theoretical route to muscle beyond training and drugs. As of 2024, Wikipedia says there is no evidence of its use in sport.[1]

paras: In 2001 Theodore Friedmann and speed-skating champion Johann Olav Koss published a first public warning about gene doping, and the IOC Medical Commission working group noted the potential for abuse.[1] Gendicine, the first approved gene-therapy drug, appeared in China in 2003; Neovasculgen and Glybera followed in 2011-2012.[1]
Wikipedia lists a 2006 German coach trial that exposed athletes' interest in gene doping, including an email seeking Repoxygen, an EPO gene therapy that had been studied in animals in 2002.[1]

Targets named in reviews include myostatin, IGF-1, EPO, VEGF and endorphin-related genes; reviews discuss the hype versus the reality of each.[1][2][3] In mice, "marathon mice" with PPAR gamma therapy had about double the endurance of controls (2004).[1]

Early detection looked for exon-exon junctions in added cDNA absent from normal genomic DNA, followed by real-time and multiplex PCR and next-generation sequencing.[1] Studies have tested direct detection of gene transfer in blood samples and the longevity of vector DNA after injection in primates.[4][5] Indirect methods are harder because natural variants can resemble doping.[1]

Viral vectors can cause immune responses, inflammation, insertional mutagenesis and death; the 1999 death of Jesse Gelsinger in a gene-therapy trial led to tighter regulation.[1] Mice overexpressing EPO developed degeneration of liver, kidney, nerve and muscle tissue.[6]

No studies found of gene doping in healthy people for performance. Gene therapies are studied clinically for disease, and reviews discuss their potential misuse in sport.[2][3] Related animal work includes the myostatin, IGF-1 and EPO studies cited above.[1][6]
